Nvidia (Buy-rated): Nvidia is a foundational enabler of physical AI, providing the full technology stack that allows robots to perceive, reason, and interact with the real world through its Isaac Gr00t humanoid foundation models, Omniverse simulation platform, and Jetson edge computing systems. The company’s strategy extends beyond silicon, positioning Nvidia as the operating platform for next-generation robotics by supplying the AI models, synthetic data tools, and simulation environments required to accelerate adoption. As physical AI transitions from research environments to large-scale deployment across factories, logistics networks, and service applications, we expect training requirements and token consumption to increase meaningfully. This should support a more durable AI investment cycle as enterprises invest in increasingly sophisticated physical AI models and infrastructure. Given its leadership across AI compute, software, and robotics platforms, we believe Nvidia is well positioned to be a key beneficiary of this trend. The funds rate cannot do much to stop cost-push inflation, and domestic sectors like the labor market, housing, and households that pay interest are not inflationary. • New Chair Kevin Warsh finds a divided FOMC to navigate as a new Chair. We project the FOMC remain on a prolonged hold into 2027. Next year, in 2027, consistent with the “balanced approach” rule we expect one 25 bp rate cut in June. The same should apply to other non-EEA pension funds rated at least AA- on a second-best rating basis (Credit Quality Step 1 or CQS1) and having a link to the public sector. Assuming Canadian pension funds are viewed as public sector entities (PSE) in accordance with Art. 116 CRR, the question is whether their debt can be treated as an exposure to the sovereign (Article 116 (4) CRR , link). For PSE outside the EEA, this is only possible if the competent authority of a third country with equivalent supervisory confirms the equivalence of risk positions with sovereign exposure. Canadian Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) seem sufficient in this respect, i.e. Section 4.1.2. allows for equal treatment of provinces and crown agents with the Canadian sovereign. However, on our understanding, Canadian pension funds are not crown agents. Hence, for Canadian pension funds , Article 116 (2) CRR seems to apply, referring Article 115(-1) CRR (link), in turn referring to the rating of the Canadian pension funds. As Canadian pension funds are rated CQS1 (i.e. at least AA- on the second-best-rating basis), a risk weight of 20% applies. There sems a risk that investors could argue that Canadian pension funds are not PSE but are corporates. records.text: Declining robot prices to bring about a crossover point Several humanoid robot manufacturers, such as UBTech, have suggested the possibility of humanoid costs dropping rapidly. As of 2026, we estimate the manufacturing cost (BOM: Bill of Materials) for industrial and research humanoid robots is around $74,000 per unit, but similar to other industrial products, this cost will likely decline significantly through mass production. We forecast the price of humanoid robots to fall from $42,000 in 2025 to $21,000 in 2035. As a result, we think we are fast approaching a “crossover point” where rising labor costs will intersect with the falling price of the robots themselves, shifting away from the current situation where robot implementation is not cost-effective. We analyze that the payback period for humanoid robots will fall to the equivalent of 2.8 years of labor costs in 2026, and to the equivalent of 1.9 years in 2027. Balance between price and performance is key We think the societal implementation of humanoid robots, which will start with the automotive industry and ripple out to other industries, will not spread to homes and streets all at once. A scenario of gradual proliferation in accordance with safety, cost, and technical maturity is likely realistic. records.text: Rising work content and operating complexity tailwind for automation The second structural driver is the expanding operating scale managed by each warehouse employee. Data shows floor area and revenue per worker increasing over time (Exhibit 32). These measures do not necessarily imply greater physical workload in isolation, but they indicate that warehouse operators must manage more activity and capacity with a more expensive labor base. Demand-side complexity compounds the pressure. MonotaRO’s expanding product line-up and inventory SKU count illustrate the growth in assortment breadth (Exhibit 33), while TRUSCO reports rising inventory items alongside higher labor cost per shipment line (Exhibit 34). Shorter delivery lead times have also shifted from a competitive differentiator toward a baseline customer requirement across manufacturing and distribution markets. More SKUs, fragmented order profiles, faster turnaround requirements, and rising labor costs make continued expansion through manual labor increasingly difficult. We therefore see the need for warehouse productivity investment as structural rather than cyclical. The remaining question is not whether automation penetration rises, but which solutions—fixed automation, AMRs, robotic manipulators or humanoids—are best suited to each remaining workflow. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 01 September 2026 How to track positioning in the futures market?: The Money Managers (MM) component captures the activity of entities that trade futures on behalf of clients – namely Commodity Trading Advisors (CTAs), Registered Commodity Pool Operators (CPOs) and unregistered funds. In base metals we use the LME Commitments of Traders Report (COTR) as the reference for market open interest. The MM metric is calculated as the five-year rolling percentile of the difference between long and short open-interest held by financial firms. Similarly, for the energy sector we adjust the ICE COT and NYMEX CFTC net futures MM position by the total market open interest. This normalisation reflects both the direction (long versus short) and the magnitude of participants’ exposure. In precious metals, although MM activity exists in futures, it is relatively small compared with exposure generated by physically backed ETFs. Consequently, changes in the assets held by precious metal ETFs provide a more reliable gauge of investor exposure than futures-based positions. How to track positioning in the options market?: The normalised spread between the implied volatility (IV) of an out of the money (OTM) call and put option captures how the market values upside versus downside risk for a commodity’s price. records.text: ab 30 August 2026 Global Research Canada Economic Perspectives Broad-based Q2 growth, BoC still on hold The Canadian economy expanded 3.3% q/q annualized in Q2, just a tenth stronger than we expected, and Q1's -0.1% contraction was revised up to a 0.3% increase. This left H1 growth at 1.8% annualized. The composition of growth was more encouraging too. Growth was supported by strong consumption, a revival in business fixed investment and net exports. The revisions to Q1 growth reflected upward revisions to exports or non-metallic minerals and energy products, both of which supported Q2 growth too. Taking on board the latest data we have revised up our expectations for real GDP to 1.1% on an annual average basis in 2026 and carried forward a little strength into 2027 taking up growth a tenth to 1.9%. We remain cognizant that the momentum in growth could be hampered by on going trade tensions with the US, which we discuss in more detail here. We are also aware of the inflation risks that retaliatory tariffs and FX movements could cause. For these reasons we expect that the Bank of Canada (BoC) will still strike a cautious tone at their meeting next Wednesday, September 2, despite the better growth picture in the Q2 data. This isn't a monetary policy report meeting but we would expect that the BoC acknowledge that Q2 GDP came in stronger than they expected. We expect they also comment on the risks from trade tensions and this likely features in the post-meeting press conference.

records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 01 September 2026 The impact of the physical market: The price pressure indicator discussed on the previous slide works well for many commodities, but in the base metal, power and gas sectors, the market is far more closely linked to physical flow. Inventories act as a barometer of the balance among production, processing and end-use demand. In this enhanced version of our Commodity Positioning framework, we have included a component that tracks the physical market. For natural gas we consider the domestic storage level, while for base metals, rather than relying on pure inventory volumes, we focus on the percentage of metal held on warrant, as this captures the true physical liquidity of the market. A rising percentage suggests an increase in immediate, tradable supply (bearish), while a falling percentage signals a tightening of available stock (bullish). In addition to the level and trajectory of inventories, the net exposure of commercial traders provides a second source of insight. The model drops the generic price pressure metric and instead uses a blend of commercial open interest and an inventory ‘scarcity’ indicator, which together reflect the core supply and demand forces that move base metal prices. In opening remarks, Chairman Warsh said that topics for the G20 meetings had shifted over the years from "secular stagnation" to "secular growth" and a "global investment surge." Vendors slow to transition from static subscription licensing to dynamic, value-based pricing risk losing market share to agile, cloud-native competitors. How will robotics accelerate share gains from brick-and-mortar retail? In our view, companies that leverage robotics and automation, especially e-commerce retailers, will be well-positioned to gain share from traditional brick-and-mortar stores by compressing the cost to serve while simultaneously improving the customer experience. Lower cost to serve: Automation allows e-commerce operators to improve service n levels while simultaneously lowering costs through reduced markdowns, lower shipping costs, and slower labor growth. For example, as highlighted earlier in the report, we present a scenario analysis around Amazon’s cost to serve where we estimate that ~5.6% of leverage in total cost to serve from automation by 2030 results in ~$72 bn in total cost savings and represents ~240 bps of margin tailwind to consolidated EBIT by 2030. records.text: M Global Idea Sunday Start | What's Next in Global Macro Inflation Is a Choice… but How Do You Choose? Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC Seth B Carpenter Chief Global Economist Seth.Carpenter@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-0370 The Fed’s Jackson Hole conference has a reputation for making news. In years past, the Fed Chair has on occasion delivered big reveals about the future course of monetary policy and its tools in ways that have moved markets. On Friday, we heard from Chair Warsh in the mountains of Wyoming, and after he reinforced the FOMC’s commitment to 2% inflation, markets reacted by pricing in more policy rate hikes. At the June press conference, Chair Warsh laid out his view that “inflation is a choice,” but he was not as clear about how that choice is made. The market reacted by pricing in more policy rate hikes by year end. Subsequent data releases have continued to shift pricing, with higher inflation implying more rate hikes and lower inflation implying fewer. Interest rates are the predominant tool, Chair Warsh said on Friday, but not the only tool, and he has been clear he would like to shrink the balance sheet. The forecast that our US team has had for no hikes this year was predicated on inflation moderating to the point where the FOMC decides against hiking at all. But the Committee decides by voting, and we have already seen three dissenting votes in favor of a hike. Constructive core view: Earnings The most compelling argument supporting a positive view on regional equities is the exceptionally strong profit growth generated by markets with high exposure to the tech hardware supply chain. We have raised our profit growth forecasts again and now expect earnings growth of 350% and 60% in Korea and Taiwan this year, followed by a further 35% and 30%, respectively, in 2027. This brings regional earnings growth to 72% and 23% for 2026 and 2027, broadly in line with the consensus aggregate forecast, albeit with some notable differences at the individual market level. Strong 1QFY26 results in Japan have also prompted us to raise our FY26 earnings growth forecast to 19% from 13%. Of note, ERLI, our earnings revision lead indicator that we publish at the start of each month, has provided consistent guidance on the direction and magnitude of consensus sell-side earnings revisions. It continues to signal a moderate pace of upgrades. Zooming out, the AsiaPac region is delivering robust profit growth following an extended period of sub-par earnings performance. As we examined in two global strategy papers (see here and here), regional earnings grew at a modest 6% CAGR from 2011 to 2025, well below the mid-teens growth rates recorded during the previous two decades. However, the 10y JGB yield may move closer to 3% in a bear market . This week, an announcement regarding budget appropriation is expected. PM T akaichi has noted a policy to limit new deficit government bonds to around ¥40trn, which is not surprising . This is because the government is likely to decide on a total size enabling it to suggest the debt-to-GDP ratio is flat or declining . That said, this figure is unlikely include bridging bonds related to the growth strategy. The burden on the JGB market will likely increase significantly. We think the actual impact on the market will be constrained by shortening issuance duration, but investors may adopt more of a wait-and-see approach in October-December, which could increase volatility. However, there is a limit to the rise in yen rates. Against the backdrop of the BoJ’s neutral rate estimates, 2.5% may be the upper limit for short-term rates. Even if long-term rates change similarly, the 10y bond yield would be around 3.5%, and it would fall below that if the curve flattens. Assuming a 10y UST yield of 5%, the spread narrowing to 150bp should be sufficient . Beta breakevens also remain attractive, as do “gamma breakevens” From time to time, we have suggested “beta breakeven” longs – combining a bullish view on Euro inflation with a bullish view on real rates, and those are worth considering now. Back in April, we recommended a variation of this, which we called a “gamma breakeven” trade – a long in 1y5y Euro inflation at 2.00%, combined with selling a 1y5y Euribor ATM payer at a strike of 2.91% for 29bp. We entered at -29bp, setting a target of +20bp and a stop at -60bp (see report: ‘Euro inflation - from "beta breaks" to "gamma breaks"?’, 15 April 2026). We saw the risk being a post-conflict slide into stubbornly sub- target inflation. Adding the bp move in the forward inflation rate to the bp value of option, since inception, gives a current value of -23bp. How this “gamma breakeven” trade looks today Exhibit 3 to Exhibit 5 show the implied evolution of the Euribor, Euro inflation and “real Euribor” curves over the next twelve months. Note the larger range for the y-scale of Exhibit 5 compared to the others. 5y Euribor is currently priced to rise by 7bp from 3.13% to 3.20% over the next twelve months and 5y inflation is priced to fall by 11bp from 2.23 to 2.12, so 5y real Euribor is priced to rise by 18bp, from 0.90% to 1.08

records.text: Noel Dixon 31 August 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General BoC Preview: Holding rates steady amidst trade tensions Just as Canada’s economy was gaining momentum, trade tensions with the US resurfaced. The new 50% Section 338 tariffs affect roughly 5% of Canadian exports to the US, while other tariffs cover an additional 3%. We do not expect this exposure to derail Canada’s underlying economic momentum or prompt the BoC to adopt a more dovish stance. July inflation also exceeded consensus expectations, and PriceStats indicates that August inflation is running above its seasonal average. We therefore expect the BoC to hold rates at its 2 September meeting. Although Governor Macklem will acknowledge trade- related risks, he is also likely to emphasize vigilance given the economy’s resilience. In our view, the dispute is weighing on key US swing states, including Maine, Michigan and Ohio, where Senate races could determine control of the chamber. This adds pressure on the Trump administration to reach an agreement around the midterms, particularly because many of the hardest-hit states are Republican-leaning or politically competitive. We therefore expect a negotiated settlement. Together with strong real-money demand, this supports our constructive medium-term outlook for the CAD. Canada’s economy has gained momentum. records.text: 31 August 2026 Germany Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 What are the chances of the capital stock being rejuvenated? There are early signs of a turnaround in the public capital stock. Expenditure from the Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality Fund has increased markedly since the beginning of the year. In addition, the recently adopted Infrastructure Accelerator Act is intended to accelerate planning and approval procedures. We expect the first positive effects on infrastructure investment to materialise towards the end of the year. But 80% of fixed investment is private and accelerating private investment is therefore critical to Germany’s future competitiveness. This is precisely where the challenge lies. Despite the cyclical recovery and improving order books, German firms continue to assess their competitive position very pessimistically. Weak perceptions of competitiveness are likely to weigh on investment incentives. After all, investment in new machinery, equipment and technologies only takes place where firms see attractive market opportunities. This creates the risk of a self- reinforcing dynamic: weaker investment slows the renewal of the capital stock and, with it, productivity growth, thereby further undermining competitiveness. The recently announced reform package therefore represents an important first step towards strengthening Germany’s competitiveness. This relationship is particularly pronounced in sectors such as pharmaceuticals and motor vehicles, where the pace of capital-embodied technological change is especially high. In these industries, new generations of machinery, equipment, patents and technologies are significantly more productive than older vintages. When investment is postponed for prolonged periods, the diffusion of new technologies slows and the gap to the technological frontier widens. In an era of rapid technological change, this can prove increasingly costly. The latest GDP details for Q2 2026 underline this concern. While the economy continued to recover, investment in machinery, equipment and vehicles, precisely those assets through which new technologies enter the production process, fell by 1.4% qoq. This suggests that the renewal of Germany's productive capital stock remains sluggish despite the cyclical upswing. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 01 September 2026 Which proxy best represents a trend-following investor?: In the previous version of our Commodity Positioning framework, we incorporated a trend component based on the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD). The MACD is an oscillating indicator widely employed in technical analysis to assess momentum, identify prevailing trends and signal potential reversals. Our methodology has since evolved. We now draw on the Global Macro CTA Tracker, whose outputs have consistently mirrored the flow patterns of trend-following investors. By integrating this tracker into the new Commodity Positioning model, we replace the MACD with an indicator of investor sentiment that provides a more robust and consistent assessment of trend dynamics. The Global Macro CTA Tracker is designed to mimic a cross-asset, systematic strategy that: 1. Identifies trends: for each asset, we compare its current price with the daily price series over the past year to generate an asset-specific trend signal. 2. Applies a vol-parity weighting: each trend signal is scaled by the asset’s recent volatility, ensuring that every asset contributes a similar amount of volatility-adjusted risk. 3. Targets a constant portfolio volatility: we assume a typical trend-following CTA aims for a fixed overall volatility; therefore, we target an annualised portfolio volatility of 8.5%. First, automobile factories and large-scale logistics hubs with a pressing need for automation will function as early adopters, and we view the ability to accumulate data there and the expected cost reductions driven by mass production will serve as catalysts for humanoids to spread to other industries. Phase 1: Automobile factories / Large-scale logistics hubs - Closed environments where safety management is easy (inside fences or restricted areas) - Mainly parts transportation, container loading/unloading, and simple picking tasks. Phase 2: General manufacturing / Small-to-medium factories / General warehouses - Decline in unit prices due to mass production effects (assumed at the $20,000 to $30,000 level per unit) Establishment of safety standards as collaborative robots, executing tasks in environments mixed with humans. Phase 3: Services / Nursing care / Infrastructure / Homes - Full-scale rollout begins in non-manufacturing sectors where labor shortages are most severe - Taking on autonomous operations in open environments where an unspecified large number of people are present. With vPLCs, the physical hardware is decoupled and vendors instead monetize the technology through software subscription licenses, consumption-based fees, and managed services. While this subscription-based, pay-per-use model may dilute upfront hardware margins, it establishes highly predictable, recurring revenue streams. It also allows vendors to capture additional value by upselling centralized edge management platforms, remote diagnostics, and advanced AI-driven analytics. Siemens has decoupled its hardware and software offerings through its Siemens Xcelerator portfolio, offering its primary vPLC product (SIMATIC S7-1500V) under an annual subscription model. Schneider has also introduced its EcoStruxure Automation Expert platform which enables software-defined automation to run on any compatible hardware. Even players that transition to SaaS might face risks though, as with generative AI democratizing industrial programming it erodes the barriers to entry into the vPLC market and increases the risks from ‘seat compression’ of traditional SaaS industrials models, given the reduced need for headcount with licences. Historically, a factory floor required dozens of physical PLCs. With virtualization, multiple vPLCs can be consolidated onto a single edge server. As AI agents optimize factory-floor workloads, the demand will shift from paying “per vPLC instance” to paying for operational outcomes

records.text: Global Commodities 01 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Super El Niño and Geopolitical Supply Risks Reinforce Our Bullish Ags View and Raise Food Inflation Risks A strengthening Super El Niño remains our highest-conviction agricultural risk heading into late 2026 and early 2027. NOAA now assigns a greater than 90% probability of a very strong event and a 69% probability that the event exceeds the strength of all El Niño episodes since 1950 during October-December (NOAA, August 2026 update). Based on our new Production-at-Risk (PAR) framework, current market pricing appears to reflect only a portion of the potential downside risks to global agricultural production. The largest weather-exposed commodities remain palm oil, robusta coffee, rice, sugar, cocoa, and Australian wheat, while risks are concentrated geographically across Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and parts of Brazil. Importantly, production revisions since March 2026 remain significantly smaller than our estimated production-at-risk metrics, suggesting additional downside risks to global supply estimates if El Niño continues to strengthen. While Argentina is likely to benefit from improved rainfall, we believe risks to global agricultural production remain skewed to the upside for prices. Figure 1. records.text: opment of humanoid robots has brought the advantages of vPLCs to the forefront of industrial automation. Unlike stationary industrial robots that rely on dedicated physical PLCs, mobile humanoids coordinate with their environments via software-defined vPLCs. This software-driven approach is essential because humanoid “brains” run on advanced AI models and computer vision algorithms powered by high-performance Systems-on-Chips (SoCs). Bridging these modern, software-defined platforms with rigid, hardware-bound physical PLCs is highly complex. vPLCs solve this integration bottleneck as they establish a centralized system which can directly control an entire fleet of mobile humanoids over high-speed virtual networks. This streamlines data exchange, simplifies the overall system architecture and enhances simultaneous coordination of distinct humanoids. Currently, the company’s SAM covers about 30% of a humanoid’s BOM. Against a backdrop of increasing robot complexity, such as the decentralization of intelligence and a rise in the number of joints and sensing needs, Renesas has outlined a plan to expand its coverage to 70% of the BOM in the long term. Renesas has a distinct advantage in its ability to leverage proven technologies from the automotive sector. In addition, beyond its broad hardware portfolio, the company’s competitive edge lies in its ability to support their customers’ development through the “Renesas 365” platform, which facilitates design optimization in a virtual environment. As many players enter the humanoid market (a market with remarkable technological evolution characterized by high-mix, low-volume production and rapid change), we believe the value of “Renesas 365” (which enables efficient design, improvement, and lifetime management on a cloud platform) could be increasingly recognized. records.text: Sanhua-H/A (2050.HK/002050.SZ, Buy/Neutral): We believe Sanhua has the potential to supply actuator assemblies to its North American customers, supported by long-standing customer relationships and a strong track record of joint R&D collaboration. However, uncertainties remain, as North American customers may choose to retain certain actuator assembly processes in-house. We believe Sanhua’s core business remains solid, underpinned by its leadership position in global EV thermal management and HVAC components. The company is well positioned to benefit from rising global EV penetration, as well as increasing HVAC demand driven by data centers and energy storage systems (ESS). We maintain a Buy rating on Sanhua-H, given its wide valuation discount of 38% versus Sanhua-A (Neutral-rated), with further upside potential from possible participation in the North American robot supply chain. Our 12-month target price for Sanhua-H/A is HK$40.0/Rmb38.6, based on a 2030E P/E of 23x/25x, discounted back to 2026E using a COE of 9.5%. What remains intact into Labor Day? Several of our highest-conviction June views have strengthened:  Dispersion remains the dominant theme.  High quality is preferable to lower-quality credit.  Refinancing-dependent borrowers are still the most vulnerable.  Security selection matters more than broad beta.  The AI financing cycle remains intact. What changes to our views? The June outlook assumed that deteriorating lower-quality fundamentals would eventually drive wider dispersion. Jackson Hole adds a second transmission mechanism: rates.  We are more constructive on leveraged loans relative to HY.  We are less constructive on long-duration IG.  We have higher conviction in BBs, and prefer Bs versus CCCs.  We see a higher probability that a Q3 repricing begins through rates and duration before spreading into broader credit markets.  Our end of Q3 spread targets turn more constructive on loans (475bps), remain unchanged for HY (275bps), and point to modest widening in IG spreads (82bps). We are now at peak fiscal support to growth. We are also at peak tariff impact on inflation and potentially peak energy shock inflation. Will energy prices fall back, or supply constraints rise? The labor market appears more vulnerable than appreciated. If the AI investment or support for equities falters, the expansion itself would be at risk. The FOMC will need to confront these risks too. The energy shock widened the distribution of potential outcomes for monetary policy (rates up and down). We have a Chair whose policy preferences are unknown. As a base case, we expect the FOMC to keep the Fed funds rate unchanged in 2026, but without much conviction. We are bullish longer-term growth and estimate that we are on the cusp of an acceleration in structural growth. While some parts of auto manufacturing are highly automated (e.g. body welding), and about a quarter of traditional industrial robots are sold to the auto industry, there are many jobs at auto OEMs and suppliers that are mostly manual (e.g. final assembly, wire harnesses) that could benefit from automation in the long-term as the technology improves. Constructive core view: Macro backdrop Our core regional equity market view remains constructive, which is why we expect the regional index to break out of its current trading range once risk appetite rebuilds. This view is based on four pillars: macro, earnings, valuation, and positioning. The macro backdrop can be summarized as fairly positive for equities. First, GDP growth is tracking broadly in line with trend levels across major regions, with global GDP growth likely to improve from 2.5% in 2026 to 2.8% next year. Second, a moderate monetary policy tightening cycle is underway in the AsiaPac region, but not to an extent that threatens growth or equity market valuations. Moreover, our economists maintain a more dovish-than-consensus view on the Fed and expect two rate cuts in 2027, which should ease pressure on regional central banks. Third, we expect moderate Asian FX appreciation vs. USD over the next 12 months, which has historically been supportive of Asian equity market performance. Finally, our Oil analysts‘ base-case view is for Brent crude to moderate from the current high-$80/bbl level to US$75/bbl in 2027, which is also fundamentally supportive for the region. records.text: Manufacturing Capacity Constraints Appear Limited to a Few Sectors Supporting the AI Buildout We also see only limited evidence of capacity constraints binding in the manufacturing sector. Exhibit 5 shows that most manufacturing industries are currently operating well below their maximum potential output, leaving room to expand production with existing capacity. We also consider a more stringent measure of spare capacity suggested by Fed economists that caps attainable utilization at each sector’s observed peak rate over recent business cycles, on the grounds that firms rarely reach reported full capacity and the highest rate achieved in practice is a more realistic ceiling.3 Even on this measure, only a few industries are nearing their limits—notably electrical equipment and machinery manufacturers, which are likely supporting the AI infrastructure buildout. Capacity utilization is not available at the sub-industry level in these two sectors, but more granular industrial production data show rapid growth in batteries, communication wire and cable, and power transmission equipment—consistent with these sectors nearing their capacity limits amid strong AI-related demand. This is why the bond divergence persists. The West's bond markets are subject to external discipline – foreign buyers who are able to leave when the fiscal story worsens. China's bond market is subject to internal capture – domestic savings that cannot leave even if they wanted to. Both are telling the truth about their respective economies. They are just answering different questions. The West's bond market is answering: what yield do global investors demand to hold this debt? records.text: However, other aspects of the auto industry are still mostly manual, including final assembly, given the physical spaces the operator needs to reach and the varied tasks that must be completed. In fact, over-automating certain jobs was a challenge that Tesla encountered with the Model 3. The auto industry is now exploring the increased use of general purpose and humanoid robots to help further improve efficiency. Growing labor constraints, including with tariff/on-shoring requirements, are adding to the demand (including at both suppliers and OEMs). Simpler tasks that are too varied to economically automate, such as in-bound parts sorting and inspection, is one area that humanoid and general purpose robots are being evaluated. Labor shortage In regions such as the US and Europe, there are many cases where a higher local parts procurement ratio is required (from an industrial protection perspective), making automobile and auto parts production necessary in regions with relatively high labor costs. Given tariff and trade policies, optimized production expansion coupled with automobiles will be an essential element in building a sustainable business structure. But the funding model that insulates China's bond market from global forces is a waning asset. It works today. It will work less well in five years. And in 10 years, China may face the same question that Japan is confronting now – what happens when the savers can no longer fund the borrowers? What the divergence is really telling us The great bond divergence is not a curiosity. It is a signal. It is telling us that the global fixed income market has fractured into two regimes with fundamentally different dynamics. In one regime – the West – bond markets are repricing for higher neutral rates, fiscal deterioration, and a shrinking external buyer base. Yields are rising because the marginal buyer demands it. In the other regime – China – bond markets are rallying despite comparable fiscal deterioration because a trapped domestic savings glut has nowhere else to go. Yields are falling because the marginal buyer has no alternative. Both regimes carry risk. PPI rose 3.6% year-on-year in Q2 – its first positive reading since late 2022. If deflation were the primary driver, we would expect Chinese bond yields to be rising as the deflationary impulse fades. They are not. The 10y yield has continued to fall even as the price data has improved. Something else is holding yields down. The deeper puzzle: fiscal The fiscal comparison is even more interesting. Because the fiscal argument, rather than explaining the divergence, deepens the puzzle. The official Chinese government debt figure is around 75% of GDP . That looks manageable.But China's fiscal system relies heavily on off-balance-sheet borrowing through local government financing vehicles; the LGFVs that have become the defining feature of Chinese public finance. records.text: Humanoid robotics will likely drive valuation multiple expansion Our US and Korean research teams apply a P/E multiple of 150x for Tesla and 60x for Robotis to their respective robotics business earnings, factoring in growth potential for humanoid robotics valuation. records.text: Looking for Pockets of Overheating We see little sign of overheating at a macroeconomic level today. The labor market is in balance and wage pressures are moderate. As the left panel of Exhibit 1 shows, our slack tracker—a composite of ten measures of labor market utilization scaled to the unemployment rate—is 1pp higher than late last cycle, when the Fed struggled to sustain 2% inflation. The right panel shows that wage growth is running below the rate we estimate is compatible with 2% inflation. Aggregate measures of industrial capacity utilization are not particularly high either. But some Fed officials have recently highlighted resource constraints connected to the AI boom as a source of inflationary pressure, which raises the broader question of whether there are pockets of overheating beneath the surface. In this week’s Analyst, we use industry-level data, including alternative data measures of utilization rates in the service sector, to assess the extent of capacity constraints. Limited Bottlenecks in the Labor Market We find few pockets of overheating in the labor market. To gauge tightness at the industry level, we calculate a jobs-workers gap for each sector—the difference between job openings and unemployed workers, scaled by the size of the sector’s labor force. As we noted in the past, this measure has captured labor market tightness better than the unemployment rate and other standard indicators in recent years. C) Korea: Two Primary Roles in the Global Robotics Ecosystem Key Enablers for Humanoid Developers (Ex-China): South Korea is uniquely positioned as a critical supply-chain partner for non-Chinese humanoid developers, leveraging its robust automotive-parts ecosystem to lead in humanoid actuator production. US-based developers are increasingly sourcing these critical components from Korean suppliers. For example, Boston Dynamics selected Hyundai Mobis to supply actuators for its next-generation Atlas humanoid, while HL Mando—already a supplier of quadruped robot actuators in the US—is preparing for a pivot into humanoid actuator mass production in the US. The country also features a mature domestic robotics ecosystem of established players and agile startups. Robotis (founded in 1999) is expanding its global footprint by preparing for mass actuator production at its new Uzbekistan facility. Additionally, South Korea has a high concentration of developers specializing in dexterous robotic hands, a capability that evolved from its strong industrial gripper manufacturing base. records.text: DISCLOSURES, PLEASE SEE PAGE 17. Global Portfolio Manager's Digest Rates, Risk and Resilience We provide context and perspective on research across regions and asset classes. This week, we focus on policy-rate repricing as Treasury market concerns ease, assess opportunities in European government bonds, and analyze how persistent drought is affecting infrastructure across Europe. • Beyond Term Premium: We have written extensively about the rise in long-end yields, its drivers and the Treasury's response. But the long-end story is now increasingly well understood. The Treasury has signaled a willingness to lean against further increases in yields, the long-end term premium has retraced from recent highs, and much ink has been spilled about its durability. As the Jackson Hole Symposium approaches, the more interesting question may no longer be where term premium goes next, but whether markets have fully repriced the path of the policy rate. We recommend tactically paying 2y SOFR at 4.08%. The market has largely accepted the possibility of further tightening. records.text: Japan’s robotics industry as a “creator” Expanding the humanoid market requires the evolution of AI capabilities and the evolution of hardware (especially the Hands). When comparing object localization + actuation across multiple AI models to human capabilities, a significant gap still exists (though the difference is narrowing). Unlike conventional LLMs that are completed in digital spaces such as text and images, the humanoid brain, which repeats cognition, judgment, and action in real time in physical space, will require breakthroughs in “data quality and quantity” as well as “model lightening/optimization (distillation).” Focus also on the development of robot hands In addition, physical AI requires “Sim-to-Real,” which involves executing actions learned on a simulator in the real world without error, along with the minimization of latency. The human hand, in particular, consists of 27 bones and numerous muscles/nerves per hand, possessing an extremely delicate control of force. Current robot hands are capable of simple actions such as grasping and placing, but tasks such as “pinching a thin wire harness with fingertips and inserting it into a narrow gap with appropriate force” are difficult. “Next-generation robot hands,” equipped with over 20 degrees of freedom per hand and high-density tactile sensors on the fingertips, are drawing attention as the next breakthrough. records.text: Case studies on role of automation & robotics in warehouses for the retail industry - Amazon and Walmart Amazon (AMZN) Amazon’s warehouse automation serves as an unlock for greater efficiency and margin expansion. Amazon is moving from singular point automation (e.g., robotic arms,pick and sort) towards system-level automation where AI coordinates the backend supply chain efforts for a warehouse. Amazon’s commentary points to fulfillment automation as a way to localize inventory, reduce distance traveled and touches per package, increase units per box, and reduce cost to serve for same-day/next-day delivery. This becomes increasingly important as Amazon is expanding speed-sensitive categories such as everyday essentials and perishables. Looking ahead, we believe Amazon remains in the early innings of extracting productivity gains from automation, robotics, and AI, providing a multi-year opportunity for shipping and fulfillment costs to grow below unit volumes and supporting continued core retail margin expansion. We expect that Amazon will continue to lower its cost to serve per unit, (defined as reported fulfillment expense excluding SBC and payment processing + shipping per unit) as management remains committed to improving efficiency levels in the Stores business. records.text: nceptualize the architecture of Foundation Models in Physical AI through a distinct three-layered framework. The World Model Layer: This layer serves as the cognitive and predictive “brain” of physical reasoning, understanding fundamental physical laws and predicting future states. Key examples include NVIDIA ’s Cosmos and Toyota’s Unified World Model (UWM). Major global technology firms, such as Google, Meta, and Tesla, are actively competing to establish dominance in this foundational layer. The Digital Twin Layer: This layer functions as the simulation, training, and validation environment (the “sandbox”). It is represented by platforms like NVIDIA ’s Omniverse and is primarily developed by factory automation (FA) giants such as Siemens, alongside various US and Chinese industrial software manufacturers. The Industrial OS Layer: This layer acts as the execution and control system (the “cerebellum”), translating high-level decisions into precise, real-time physical actions and motor control. This is equivalent to NVIDIA ’s Isaac platform. Under this framework, we categorize the Large Behavior Model (LBM) recently demonstrated by Toyota as a key technology belonging to this Industrial OS layer. 31 August 2026 18 Goldman Sachs Japan Automobiles For the exclusive use of CAYLA.BUETTNER@BLUECRESTCAPITAL.COM 7595159db82544668b3260609400172c

records.text: 2 Euro Area Viewpoint | 01 September 2026 Back to school, Sep-26 edition Forecast update: better carryovers vs higher energy prices and real yields We updated our forecasts summer break. We now expect Euro area GDP to grow 0.8% this year (+30bp), 1.1% in 2027 (-20bp) and 1.1% in 2028 (unch). Changes reflect better carryovers from 1H26 and a marginal lowering of the sequential growth path on the back of higher energy prices and real yields. Our inflation forecasts move to 2.9% in 2026 (+30bp), 2.2% in 2027 (+50bp) and stay at 1.8% in 2028, with core at 2.3%, 2.1% (+10bp, each) and 1.8% (unch), respectively. Headline inflation is likely to hover around 3.3-3.5% over the winter before falling below 2% in 2H26 again. Core inflation is unlikely to move higher from here. We actually expect a gradual decline to 2% by mid-27 and slightly lower thereafter. We continue to expect core inflation and broad second-round effects to remain contained. Instead, we stick to our view that insufficient aggregate demand and tight policy will ultimately lead to an inflation undershoot. Continuous advancements in physical AI are accelerating the development of humanoid robots, with an increasing number of players transitioning toward larger-scale prototypes and commercial production. Accordingly, we raise our 2035 unit sales forecast to 6.48 mn units from 1.38 mn previously. We now project the market size will reach $138 billion (approximately ¥22 tn) by 2035, compared with our previous estimate of around ¥6 tn. While Japanese companies have secured an estimated 30-40% global market n share in the FA (Factory Automation) sector, they lag significantly in the humanoid sector, where US, Chinese, and South Korean companies are actively working to establish early mass production systems. Nevertheless, Japan has a strong foundation in robotics, ranking fourth globally in industrial robot density and second only to South Korea in receptiveness to robotics adoption. Furthermore, Japan’s well-developed automotive and auto parts supply chain provides a solid foundation for the mass production of actuators and other critical robot hardware components. We believe the automotive industry, which mass-produces one of the world’s n most complex industrial products at scale, is uniquely positioned to support the mass production of humanoid robots. records.text: Key risks to our view Excessive expectations for on-site data/master craftsmanship: The accumulation of high-quality on-site data will likely play an important role in reproducing master craftsmanship. However, the foreseeable scope of applications for humanoids is relatively close to simple tasks, with a broad base. If efforts are focused on reproducing master craftsmanship, there is a risk of overlooking a massive potential market. Reliance on overseas Foundation models: By quickly adopting open Foundation models, it is possible to speed up humanoid development. However, there are debates over whether they will remain open forever and whether the expansion of the digital deficit can be tolerated, presenting a risk that external reliance is not a sustainable business model. Strong successful experiences in FA: The Japanese manufacturing industry has succeeded in the FA sector with relatively simple, repetitive tasks in mass production processes. However, the world of humanoids requires multipurpose and zero-shot responses by fully utilizing AI capabilities. There is a risk that successful experiences in FA will not necessarily be valued. Moreover, the budget assumes a significant increase in tax revenue that relies on changes to tax law. These changes, however, are likely to be vetoed by the President. This week's inflation print, if it surprises to the downside, may add to pressure on the PLN, as it would strengthen the case for a more dovish NBP . records.text: ...Translates into an Improved Margin Profile Assuming ~5.6% of leverage in cost to serve from 2026E to 2030E, we expect a total cost savings of ~$72 bn from robotics and automation efforts. We estimate ~80% of these savings to be in opex (defined as reported fulfillment expense excluding SBC and payment processing) and ~20% to be in COGS (shipping), which ultimately translates to a ~240 bps margin tailwind in consolidated EBIT by 2030 (with ~50bps of that coming from GM). A lower cost-to-serve does more than simply reduce expenses, it improves Amazon’s unit economics. This dynamic is particularly powerful given Amazon’s scale, where modest reductions in per-unit cost to serve (~11%) translates to a more significant impact to bottom line (400 bps retail EBIT margin tailwind by 2030E). Improved economics also provides Amazon with greater strategic flexibility, whereby they can choose to reinvest profits into faster delivery speeds, lower consumer prices, or enhanced Prime benefits. In our view, fulfillment efficiency is increasingly becoming a competitive differentiator rather than simply a cost center. As Amazon deploys robotics, AI-powered inventory placement, and autonomous warehouse technologies across its network, the gap between Amazon’s fulfillment economics and those of smaller eCommerce competitors may continue to widen. records.Author: Pierfrancesco Mei
records.text: We see little sign of overheating at a macroeconomic level today. The labor n market is in balance, wage pressures are moderate, and overall industrial capacity utilization is not particularly high. But some Fed officials have highlighted resource constraints connected to the AI boom as a source of inflationary pressure, which raises the broader question of whether there are pockets of overheating beneath the surface. We use industry-level data, including alternative data measures of utilization rates in the services sector, to assess the extent of capacity constraints. We find few pockets of overheating in the labor market. Across most industries, n the jobs-workers gap has fallen below its pre-pandemic level, and in the few industries where it remains somewhat elevated, such as wholesale trade and healthcare, it has eased significantly from its pandemic peak. Nor do we find signs of regional labor shortages: our new measure of tightness and wage pressures based on Beige Book commentary sits roughly in line with its historical average across all 12 Fed Districts. records.text: A prominent concern among investors is that humanoid robotics providers might bypass traditional automation incumbents by directly integrating vPLCs into their proprietary platforms. While this vertical integration could theoretically enable humanoid vendors to control deployment and command higher margins through a unified Robotics-as-a-Service (RaaS) model, such a scenario may not be plausible for various structural reasons: A humanoid robot is an autonomous agent designed to coexist and communicate n with a factory’s infrastructure and not to control it. Since factory machinery is built, commissioned, and warranted by specialized OEMs using established control architectures, it is more practical for humanoids to interface with existing systems via standard protocols rather than for robotics vendors to reverse-engineer and assume liability for the factory’s entire legacy control layer. Industrial safety is governed by uncompromising international standards (such as n SIL3/PL e) that have been developed over decades. For a humanoid startup, achieving the necessary functional safety certifications to control factory-wide heavy machinery, light curtains, and emergency stops represents a steep and cost-prohibitive barrier to entry. Modern manufacturers are actively transitioning to open software standards to n escape proprietary ecosystems. Against that backdrop, model scale is moving higher, with the discussion around larger stacks in the c.40B-80B range vs. smaller single-digit-billion-parameter to 20B pre-training systems. Model players argue that multiple rounds of iteration are still ahead before these stacks are deployment-ready withconsistent quality. High-quality, real-world, multi-dimensional data remains the primary bottleneck to practical deployment, but the discussion has clearly moved beyond broad “data recipe” debates toward what scalable data acquisition architecture can reliably produce that data. Within that shift, human-centric and ego-centric collection increasingly looks like the preferred real-world collection method for high-fidelity data, especially where companies care about preserving natural motion, contact-rich interaction, and cross-embodiment transfer. Based on what we’ve observed during 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC), there is a growing emphasis on model engineering capability, scientific data collection methodologies, effective data frames, and efficient conversion into high-quality, usable data, underscoring a constructive balance between scalability, cost, and quality. The long-term moat is proprietary, deployment driven data. Locomotion and navigation algorithms are largely solved through simulation‑driven reinforcement learning. However, real‑world manipulation parameters (e.g., those tied to deformable objects, food preparation, tool use) are fundamentally un-simulatable and therefore data‑constrained. As a result, world model companies orient their research and capital toward tasks where real‑world interaction is unavoidable and where labor displacement potential is highest. Two examples: Physical Intelligence has detailed a closed‑loop system in which human‑operated 1. robots generate video and action data for specific tasks, models are retrained and validated on live robots, and subsequent deployments generate incremental proprietary data. Critically, this proprietary dataset improves with each deployment, reinforcing management’s view that data accumulation is the primary competitive advantage. Why do physical PLCs still dominate? What are the risks associated with vPLCs? Despite the rapid rise of software-defined automation, traditional physical PLCs remain superior to vPLCs in certain critical areas, explaining why they have not yet been fully replaced by virtual alternatives. These include latency, safety and complexity of deployment. Latency and determinism. Physical PLCs run on dedicated hardware with a n real-time operating system which guarantees precise, deterministic, millisecond-level execution loops (typically 1-10 ms). By contrast, vPLCs operate on shared compute infrastructure where they must share CPU cycles with other applications. While vPLCs offer performance close to traditional PLCs, the introduction of virtualisation can result in additional and sometimes unpredictable latency. This poses a significant challenge for real-time applications that necessitate ultra-high-speed, synchronized response times such as high-speed motion control systems or high-speed packaging. Functional safety and reliability. Hosting multiple vPLCs on a single edge server n introduces a potential single point of failure. Historically, market-leading automation providers such as Siemens, Rockwell Automation, Mitsubishi Electric, and Schneider Electric, have sold PLCs under a hardware-centric business model, requiring a dedicated physical controller for each machine or robot. This architecture inherently creates vendor lock-in, forcing manufacturers to purchase proprietary hardware and rely on the vendor’s closed software ecosystems for programming and maintenance. Virtual PLCs (vPLCs) perform the same real-time control functions as traditional PLCs but are entirely software-defined. When a new assembly line needs to be controlled, traditional PLCs oblige operators to buy new hardware which needs to be mounted inside electrical cabinets and wired to machinery. By contrast, vPLCs allow operators to deploy a new “PLC” when needed without installing new physical controllers. This confers various advantages: 1) vPLCs can run on standard, off-the-shelf computer servers, or on the cloud, meaning operators are not locked into a proprietary hardware ecosystem and can mitigate supply chain risks, 2) manufacturers can expand production lines and scale capacity at lower capex, 3) operators can update control logic remotely from a centralised console, reducing the need for on-site engineers. The rapid development of humanoid robots has brought the advantages of vPLCs to the forefront of industrial automation. records.text: Japan's domestic funding model is now showing cracks for the first time in a generation. JGB yields are rising – the 30y above 4%, the 10y at a 28y high – in part because the Bank of Japan is stepping back, but also because the demographic structure that generated the savings surplus is eroding. Japan's population has been declining since 2008. The savings rate has fallen. The captive buyer base is shrinking. China is perhaps 10 to 15 years behind Japan on that demographic curve – but the curve is steepening faster. China's population has declined for four consecutive years. Fewer than 8mn babies were born in 2025 – the lowest in decades. The working-age population is contracting. The 4-2-1 problem – one child expected to support two parents and four grandparents – is no longer theoretical. As China's population ages, the savings rate will likely fall. Retirees draw down savings rather than accumulate them. Healthcare and pension costs rise. The domestic pool of capital available to fund government debt shrinks precisely as the debt continues to grow. China's augmented debt is projected to reach 146% of GDP by 2028. If the savings rate begins to decline in earnest over the same period, the model that keeps yields at 1.70% comes under pressure. That is not to suggest that a Chinese bond crisis is imminent. records.text: To illustrate the robotics used in Amazon’s warehouses we lay out their recent initiatives and note their post-COVID build out has significantly accelerated (Exhibit 42). We also note Amazon’s comments around improved efficiency at their 12th-generation fulfillment center design that incorporates robotics inventions and simplifies stowing, picking, packing and shipping. This sped up fulfillment by 25% and increased the number of items they can offer same or next day by 25%. More recently, Amazon disclosed that it has deployed its over 1 million robots, across more than 300 facilities, and launched DeepFleet, a generative AI foundation model intended to improve robot fleet travel efficiency by 10%. records.text: PM summary Humanoids have significant growth potential We are significantly raising our demand forecasts for the humanoid robot market. We raise our 2035 unit sales forecast to 6.48 mn units from 1.38 mn units previously. We project the market size will reach $138 bn (approximately ¥22 tn) in 2035, compared to our previous estimate of around ¥6 tn. This upward revision is driven by the continuous improvement of physical AI technology, with humanoid robots from several makers increasingly transitioning toward larger-scale prototypes and commercial production. Furthermore, the industry is benefiting significantly from new open-source tools, rising funding, and government support. In addition, increasing deployments are expected to generate a positive flywheel effect, where robots in operation help gather real-world data to further train and improve AI software. Consequently, we believe that robotics, including humanoids, will become more general-purpose in utility over time. Close connection between robotics and the automotive industry Automobile production bases, which possess a certain level of financial strength and have a pressing need for automation, will likely be early adopters. records.text: What may or may not get disrupted from general purpose robotics Wages of workers in warehouse & logistics roles We believe a key focus for investors in evaluating the economic effect of humanoid robots includes areas of disruption. Given that many of the early pilot deployments of humanoids are in warehouse and logistics roles, we believe one main vector of analysis relates to human employment in hand laborer and material movers roles. Importantly, US government data suggests there may be a shortage of workers in these areas, with the US BLS (Bureau of Labor and Statistics) noting that it believes there will be on average ~1.0 mn job openings per year in hand laborer and material mover roles from 2024 to 2034. Per the BLS, many of those openings are driven by the need to replace workers who transfer to different occupations or exit the labor force (e.g. retire). General purpose robotics therefore may not lead to direct job losses in aggregate in the near to intermediate term, but could impact new openings and the roles of human workers. As of 2024, there were approximately ~6.4 mn people employed in the US as hand laborers and material movers (across all industries, with 987K of those in the warehousing and storage) per the BLS. This 6.4 mn breaks out into ~3.0 mn as laborers for freight, stock, and material movers by hand; 46.5K as machine feeders and offbearers; 592K as hand packers and packagers; and 2.8 mn as stockers & order fillers. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 01 Sep 2026 11:51:04 ET │ 17 pages Global Commodities ICE Softs Outlook: Weather Risks Intensify Across Softs, with Sugar Remaining Our Highest-Conviction Bullish View CITI'S TAKE Weather risks are becoming increasingly important across the ICE softs complex, but market outcomes remain highly differentiated by inventory levels and balance sheet dynamics (see Figures 3-6). For sugar, tightening inventories, India's unexpected import program, and deteriorating weather across India, Thailand and the EU reinforce our bullish view as global balances continue to tighten. In cocoa, weather risks are also rising across West Africa, Indonesia and Ecuador, but recovering inventories and subdued grindings provide a meaningful buffer against moderate supply disruptions. We shift to more neutral-bearish on Arabica coffee as El Niño- related risks are emerging across key robusta-producing regions and inventories remain historically low, stronger Brazilian exports and improving global supply prospects should gradually ease market tightness. Overall, we continue to see the greatest upside risk in sugar. We remain bullish on sugar and raise our price targets to $0.19/lb in 3 months and $0.22/lb in 12 months. records.text: Our New Measure of Services Capacity Constraints Also Shows Limited Pressures While the Fed provides estimates of capacity utilization for the manufacturing, mining, and utilities sectors—which together account for roughly 15% of the economy—the statistical agencies do not provide comparable estimates for other sectors. The ISM publishes a semi-annual survey of nonmanufacturing operating rates, but its low frequency limits its usefulness as a timely gauge of tightness, and its interpretation is complicated because it relies on a single generic survey question rather than concrete operational measures that best capture capacity in each industry, as we previously noted. To obtain a broader gauge of capacity constraints across the economy, we draw on alternative data—including measures our equity analysts regularly use to monitor sector activity, such as transportation load factors and hotel occupancy rates—to estimate capacity utilization across seven services industries that together account for about 30% of GDP . Exhibit 7 summarizes the measures we use to proxy utilization in each of these industries. records.text: The Japanese government’s ambitious robotics strategy Setting ambitious targets The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry expects the overall market for multi-purpose robots, including humanoids, to grow to around ¥60 tn globally by 2040, and aims for Japanese companies to capture a 30% share, or ¥20 tn, of this market. In the AI Robotics Strategy revised on June 30, 2026, it outlines (1) introducing approximately 10 mn AI robots domestically as a societal implementation target for 2040, and (2) introducing 350,000 units as a medium-term milestone for 2030. The five leading sectors will be “manufacturing,” “construction and civil engineering,” “architecture,” “retail,” and “security.” At the same time, the Japanese government has secured budget to support the development of the “brains” and “bodies” of robots that move autonomously in the real world. The industries where the Japanese government aims to strategically introduce AI robots—such as construction, manufacturing, and retail—account for approximately 40% of the total workforce in Japan. Among these, tasks highly suited for robotization have been identified, including clerical work, sales, services, production, transportation, construction, and cleaning/packaging. Consequently, the immediate addressable market is expected to reach a scale equivalent to a workforce of 26 mn people. Impact on PLCs Overview The rapid development of humanoid robots has brought the advantages of virtual Programmable Logic Controllers (vPLCs) to the forefront of industrial automation. Both virtual and physical PLCs act as industrial computers to control and monitor manufacturing processes. However, while traditional PLCs are physically wired inside stationary control cabinets at specific workstations, vPLCs are entirely software-defined, enabling them to run as a centralized system commanding entire fleets of robots. The global TAM for PLCs stood at an estimated c.$13bn in 2025 and is expected to grow at c.4% CAGR over the coming years (GSe and third party sources Mordor Intelligence, Precedence Research, Global Market Insights), in line with historical growth rates (see Jacqueline Du’s PLC note here). The US midterm elections will be held on November 3, roughly two months from now and near the midpoint of the remaining period to year-end. Our US strategy team has shown that policy uncertainty and S&P 500 volatility typically rise ahead of midterm elections. These tend to moderate after the elections, leading the equity market to trade sideways beforehand and rally thereafter. We have conducted a similar analysis for the MXAPJ Index (although with a shorter data set) and find that the region also tends to range trade in the two months leading up to the election and rally during the subsequent three months. The region typically enjoys positive seasonality in the fourth quarter, but returns in midterm election years have been somewhat stronger than usual. This informs our view on the index path and implementation strategies, as discussed later. records.text: Executive Summary Traditional robotics have been successful at automating certain tasks, but limits with respect to software capability and hardware flexibility have historically constrained adoption to certain areas that are more repetitive in nature. We expect this to change going forward due to physical AI. Physical AI, per Nvidia, is what enables machines such as robots and AVs to perceive, understand, and perform complex actions in the physical world. Physical AI technology for robots is improving, and humanoid robots from several providers are increasingly set to move into larger scale prototypes and toward commercial production. This is being enabled in part as companies gather real world data to train AI software, including for both general reasoning and specific tasks (such as how to pick up an envelope or break an egg), which can’t be done simply with digital data from the internet. The industry is also befitting from new open-sourced tools, rising funding, and government support. We also believe increasing deployments can help drive a positive flywheel effect, with the robots in operation helping gather data to further train and improve AI software. We believe this can support robotics becoming more general purpose in utility over time, including humanoids. As a result of progress for the industry, and reflecting company specific plans, we’re increasing our humanoid market forecast. records.text: The frontier of robotics tech – humanoids and foundational models AI technology continues to improve with focus areas including data collection, world models and safety AI model performance continues to improve. One measure of progress with AI models is the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), which is a generalized benchmark intended to capture the overall capability of AI models by aggregating performance across several established tests covering reasoning, coding, math, and language. Unlike individual benchmarks which can saturate as models approach near‑perfect scores, ECI adjusts for task difficulty and combines results to show relative differentiation across models and over time. Higher scores indicate broader capability, while models optimized for specific tests may perform well on individual benchmarks but rank lower on ECI due to limited generalization. Models launched in 2023 were scoring around the low to mid 120s range, while models released in 2026 (GPT-5.4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6) are scoring in the mid to high 150s range. It’s also key to contextualize these scores relative to human benchmarks. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) details how AI models have improved over time and compared to humans, most recently in their 2026 AI index report. Motion Control/robot companies focus more on whole-body control and n locomotion with impressive learning and demonstrations of different physical capabilities. These companies have increasingly shifted from traditional dynamics control to reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm paradigms, while rapid domestic supply chain iterations have boosted joint power density, strengthening the dynamic adaptability and self-recovery capabilities of all-electric humanoids. The technology advancement in 2026 YTD are reflected in two key areas: (1) the deep integration of Whole-Body Control (WBC) has been bridging the gap between locomotion and manipulation, enabling robots to perform continuous upper-limb tasks while moving, such as wiping while walking or catching objects without slowing down; and (2) peak performance has improved materially, with outdoor running speeds surging to 5–6 m/s compared to last year’s 2–3 m/s, paired with much smoother motion transitions during high-frequency tasks. The primary threat of vPLCs to established players is the disruption of the legacy hardware-software lock-in. With vPLCs, customers can choose to run high-performance control logic on open, commodity servers rather than being forced to purchase expensive proprietary hardware from a single vendor. The core components of a traditional PLC system that may be disrupted include: Controller (CPU): the central processing unit of a traditional PLC system which n executes user-written control logic. In a vPLC, these proprietary hardware processors are replaced by software runtime engines running on standard edge servers or industrial PCs. Rather, a $51trn domestic savings pool, constrained by capital controls and facing a lack of attractive alternatives, has nowhere else to go. The bond market is not making a statement about China's creditworthiness. It is reflecting the reality of a closed financial system with too much savings. And it is signaling that neither real nor financial assets in China are attractive enough to absorb those savings. As a result, they end up in the bond market, even at very low yields. The Japan precedent This is not without historical parallel. Japan has maintained government debt above 200% of GDP for over a decade without experiencing a bond market crisis. The explanation is the same: domestic savings fund the government. Japanese households and institutions (especially the BoJ) hold the vast majority of JGBs. The money is domestic, the liabilities are in yen, and the savings rate – while now declining – sustained the model for decades. A common argument is that Japan owes money to itself. China is running the same playbook. The debt is large and growing, but it is funded internally, denominated in renminbi, and supported by a savings rate that is far higher any Western economy. records.text: • Running Dry: Europe is experiencing one of its hottest and driest summers on record. Western Europe recorded its warmest June-July on record, and drought conditions have spread across much of Western, Central and parts of Eastern Europe, creating risks for agriculture, industrial supply chains and energy systems. records.text: n discipline; Western bond markets (eventually) should keep government profligacy in check. China's risk is deferred and structural: what happens when the demographics turn, the savings rate falls, and the captive buyer base can no longer absorb the issuance? For global investors, the implication is that one cannot treat "bonds" as a single asset class any longer. The forces driving US Treasuries, JGBs, OATs, and Chinese government bonds are not just different in degree – they are different in kind. A view on global fixed income now requires a view on funding models, demographic trajectories, and capital account regimes, not just inflation and central bank policy. The 300bp gap between China and US fixed income is not a mispricing. It is two bond markets telling two different truths about two different systems. In the West, the external buyers are leaving and yields must rise to attract new ones. In China, the domestic savers are trapped and yields can stay low until the savers themselves start to disappear. One divergence is cyclical. The other is demographic. Both come with their own sets of problems. 30 August 2026 4 Barclays | Thinking Macro

With vPLCs, customers can choose to run high-performance control logic on open, commodity servers rather than proprietary hardware from a single vendor. Core components of a traditional PLC system that may be disrupted include the controller, the physical racks, and the physical input/output modules. What are virtual PLCs and how do they compare to standard PLCs? A Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) is a microprocessor-based industrial computer engineered to control and monitor manufacturing processes. Since their introduction in the late 1960s, PLCs have served as the backbone of factory automation, executing real-time control logic to ensure the seamless coordination of assembly lines and machinery. At its core, a PLC acts as the central orchestrator, continuously monitoring inputs from field sensors, processing this data according to a user-defined program, and executing precise commands to drive outputs such as motors, valves and actuators. For example, on a robotic assembly line, while an individual robot utilizes its own dedicated controller to manage precise joint movements, a PLC will sit above the controller, coordinating the robot’s actions with surrounding equipment such as conveyors and safety barriers. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 01 September 2026 Construction of the positioning score: Our positioning indicator yields a single value that ranges from –50 (extremely short) to +50 (extremely long). A rising positive score reflects the expansion of long exposure, whereas a deepening negative score indicates that short exposure is being added. A score of 0 represents a neutral stance: exposure is stable and at its median level over the most recent five-year window. For illustrative purposes, Figure 1 uses copper as an example. Scores above +35 or below –35 are regarded as extreme, signalling that the market is heavily long or short and therefore vulnerable to sharp price moves when fundamentals, macroeconomic news or risk appetite shift abruptly. Scores that fall between –10 and +10 are considered neutral, indicating a balanced level of exposure with relatively low market pressure. The overall score equally weights five components: trend, money managers, skew, price pressure/commercials and curve components. Each component is explained in detail in the next section. Distribution of positioning scores: For each of these inputs we compute its percentile rank within the preceding five years. This approach anchors the metric to its actual historical distribution, which is often bimodal, positively skewed and heavy-tailed (Figure 2). With this report our global research teams (across the automotive, technology & industrial landscape) examine how the landscape for physical AI has evolved across hardware, software, and semiconductors. On the back of that work, we are raising our humanoid robot market forecast. The global market is now projected to reach approximately 890,000 units by 2030 and 6.5 million units by 2035 (representing a $138 billion market opportunity). Across the report, we make a series of key conclusions to highlight for investors: Logistics and warehouse operations serve as the primary early adopters for n general-purpose humanoids. eCommerce/Retail companies (like Amazon and Walmart) are leading this transition. We frame ~5.6% of leverage in Amazon’s total cost to serve via automation by 2030, which is estimated to yield a ~$72 billion cost savings and a ~240 bps EBIT margin tailwind in our upside analysis from a wider deployment of robotics. While automotive body welding is highly automated, final assembly and parts n sorting remain manual. Automakers are actively exploring humanoids to mitigate labor challenges. records.text: option captures how the market values upside versus downside risk for a commodity’s price. We calculate this skew by first taking the difference between the 3-month IV of a 110% moneyness call and the 3-month IV of a 90% moneyness put, and then dividing that difference by the at-the-money (ATM, 100%) IV. This scaling is crucial, as a raw 2% spread might be significant when overall volatility is low but virtually meaningless when the market is already highly volatile. By normalizing with the ATM IV, we dampen the effect of volatility-regime shifts, making the metric comparable across assets and over time. A positive normalised skew means the call IV exceeds the put IV, indicating that participants price upside risk more aggressively than downside risk and suggesting upward pressure. Conversely, a negative value points to a bias toward downside risk. The chance that the ECB exceeds 2.5% depo seems to be rising. Last week’s ECB accounts for July showed some members “argued that rates needed to move into mildly restrictive territory”. In DV01 terms, 10yr+ issuance is projected to account for 42% of conventional supply, up from 27% during July-August. records.text: tly priced to rise by 7bp from 3.13% to 3.20% over the next twelve months and 5y inflation is priced to fall by 11bp from 2.23 to 2.12, so 5y real Euribor is priced to rise by 18bp, from 0.90% to 1.08%. And selling a 1y5y ATM Euribor payer at a 3.20% strike would provide a premium of 30bp. So the same strategy of entering a 1y5y Euro inflation long and selling a Euribor payer now would mean that the premium provides a cushion down to 1.82%, if the option is not exercised. And if it is, the new received 5y real Euribor position would be “protected” up to a rate of 1.38%. Once again, we would be comfortable with either outcome. The underlying appeal of the trade is the belief that euro inflation is unlikely to slide back into a “lowflation” era – that was defined by a set of secular forces that we think have passed. However, we also believe that the ECB will not need to raise real policy rates as aggressively as priced in order to check inflation. The reason to consider such trades nearer the front of the curve now is that we believe it will continue to be dominated by actual inflation and policy rate expectations and be less prone to term premium uncertainty farther along the curve.
