Short positions covered: Price depreciation paired with rising open interest signifies aggressive short positioning. 3. Short positions added: Price appreciation paired with falling open interest signifies short covering. 4. Long positions liquidated: Price depreciation paired with falling open interest signifies long liquidation. We aggregate the strength of implied position changes over an average of 1-, 3- and 6-month windows to determine a positioning trend. We incorporate the magnitude of price changes and open interest changes. These are adjusted for the implied position change (±1) and scenarios 1 and 3 given a weight of 1, while scenarios 2 and 4 are given a weight of 0.5. We believe that the components for rotary and linear actuators currently face limited supply bottlenecks, thanks to the dynamic domestic manufacturing ecosystems. However, the dexterous hand remains a universally recognized challenge in terms of technical maturity and cost reduction. While the presence of dexterous hands grew visibly since 2025 with more players entering the market, dexterous hand technology routes remain fragmented, with no consensus on the optimal configuration. records.text: Declining robot prices to bring about a crossover point Several humanoid robot manufacturers, such as UBTech, have suggested the possibility of humanoid costs dropping rapidly. As of 2026, the manufacturing cost (BOM: Bill of Materials) for industrial and research humanoid robots is estimated to be around $74,000 for high spec units, but similar to other industrial products, this cost will likely decline significantly through mass production. With BOM costs likely to decline, we forecast the price of humanoid robots on average to fall from over $40,000 in 2025 (and about $150,000 for high-spec robots) to about $21,000 in 2035 (and about $50,000 on average for high-spec robots). As a result, in applications where the technology is ready, we think the market will approach a “crossover point” where rising labor costs meet the falling price of the robots, shifting away from the current situation where robot implementation is not cost-effective. We forecast that the cost of factory-use humanoid robots will fall to the equivalent of 2.8 years of labor costs in 2026, and to the equivalent of 1.9 years in 2027 (assuming applications where the robotics technology is prepared for the task). Spending has slowed on net from the robust pace of 2024, but not nearly as much as real disposable income growth. • Households across all income groups expect to be more sensitive to future inflation now than in 2022. At the same time, households are less able to weather inflation. Households below the top 20% of the income distribution have relatively low levels of liquid assets. • Equity market wealth in Q4 was an all-time high share of household wealth (35%) and has accounted for all of the gains in wealth the last few years. The S&P 500 helps. • We have seen a ~$60 billion boost to tax refunds, thanks to the OBBBA, so we should be at the peak fiscal support for spending. The key question beyond that: Can spending keep outpacing income to this degree? The negative impact of rising rates on corporate earnings is limited, and the benefits of cost pass-throughs and capex expansion outweigh the drag. While the impact of past rate increases has only gradually materialized due to lags in loan contract resets, the cumulative effect of long-term rate increases combined with a more meaningful rise in short-term rates means corporate interest expenses are expected to peak in FY2026-27. Even at the peak, however, the drag on operating profit is expected to remain below 1ppt per year (Figure 10I m p a c t o f R a t e H i k e s b y T O P I X S e c t o r ( T O P I X E x c l u d i n g F i n s ) ). Meanwhile, cost pass-throughs and capex expansion continue to advance under economic normalization, with Japanese companies’ operating profit growing at an average annual rate of around 14% in FY2023-26. Ongoing improvements in ROIC and balance sheet reforms mean that accelerating profit growth should more than absorb the negative impact. Last week, media reports suggested that Oman and Iran reached a deal for an agreed route through the Strait of Hormuz, and President Donald Trump also highlighted that flow is increasing through the strait. These headlines provided some relief to crude prices – at least until concerns arose regarding Russia’s reported intention to escalate the war in Ukraine. The main pressure in the energy complex, however, seems to be the tightness in refinery products and European gas rather than crude oil. Low storage levels in Europe appear to be feeding the TTF market. We believe increased LNG supply in winter and a partial return of Middle East energy will be enough to balance the market eventually, especially if the El Niño impact leads to a warmer and wetter winter in Europe (see EU gas: Tight, risky – but not panicky, 24 August). Canada faces a different challenge. Its comparative advantages lie in energy, critical minerals, and other upstream sectors where investment horizons are measured in years rather than quarters. A broader agreement that cements strategic alignment could strengthen Canada's position, while increasingly conditional market access could redirect marginal investment toward the US or Mexico. The economic transmission of tariff risk may therefore be evolving. While this is not our base case, the recent escalations involving both Canada and Brazil highlight the policy uncertainty that remains. That uncertainty is compounded by the risk of prolonged disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, which could challenge our expectations for disinflation and a broader capex cycle in 2027. The bull case for 2027 currently envisions a broadening out of capex with softer inflation - both come under pressure should the outlook be adversely affected by either scenario. Continued uncertainty in the investment sphere could delay the recovery of non-AI capex in the United States and, potentially, AI Capex as the build out increasingly pivots from construction to implementation. Catalyst.Metric: AI-driven cycle and humanoid robot component demand

records.text: une 8 report, we believe the current AI-driven cycle in the Japan electronic components/semiconductors sector could be one of the biggest and longest ever, characterized by the ongoing technological evolution in AI server infrastructure followed by a wave of device proliferation (physical AI/edge AI including humanoid robots). We believe components will be just as critical to this second wave of device proliferation as they are to the first wave of AI infrastructure. Consequently, the proliferation of humanoid robots represents a potential structural growth driver for the component supply chain in Japan. Below, we map key business opportunities across drive parts, batteries, passive components, and interconnects. ECB: risks of a Dec-26 hike, cuts delayed to summer-27 Markets have repriced on higher energy prices, now expecting a bit more than two further ECB hikes and no cuts after. We see that as too hawkish. September remains our base case, but December, while an increasing possibility, is not. Crucially, we still expect the ECB to pivot to cuts in the summer of 2027, taking the deposit rate back to around or below 2% by end-2027. Germany: reform agenda at risk Core countries are creating more headaches now than the periphery. In Germany, growth looks back on track for 1% per year in 2026/27 – that’s good news. But the reform agenda announced in early July is at risk again. That increases the fragility of the federal ruling coalition again ahead of potentially complicated September state elections. France: it’s hard to be upbeat OATs have come under pressure over the summer. Our colleagues argue supply dynamics are at play. Economic weakness went beyond our expectations in 1H26. And while the economy is less dependent on gas, the price effect on consumers is still sizeable into the fall. Upcoming budget negotiations and the 2027 election cycle make it hard to see any durable relief for France over the next year (and possibly beyond).
